Stage 3 · Reading

The rules nobody explains

Four strange workplace rules, and what a careful reader can work out about each of them.

💼🔍
1 · Before you read. Look at the title. Why do you think companies leave rules unexplained?

Choose one and say which kind of company it would apply to. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say which kind of company it would apply to before you read.Choose one and note which kind of company it would apply to. You will check it against the texts.

The rules nobody explains

Written for this course. Parking guidance from the UK Health and Safety Executive, Workplace Transport Safety.

1Every organisation has at least one rule that nobody on the staff can account for. A German manufacturer insists on drivers reversing into every space in the car park. A firm in Osaka does not allow anybody to leave the building during the lunch break. A London agency once told its people that personal calls made at a desk would count against them at the annual review. A Rotterdam warehouse requires two signatures on a form that only one person ever reads. None of the four ever explained why, and in three of them the rule still applies to visitors as well as to employees.

2Turn them round, though, and they become readable. The parking rule must have begun as a safety measure rather than a matter of neatness. Britain’s Health and Safety Executive advises that where a site cannot be laid out for drive-through parking, the arrangements should encourage reverse parking, precisely because reversing out into a flow of moving traffic is where the collisions happen. Somebody at that plant may well have read the same guidance. The rule can’t have been invented to make the yard look tidy: a company that only wanted tidiness would not have troubled to enforce it on visitors.

3The legal background makes the reasoning tighter. An employer who exposes staff to a risk that could reasonably have been designed out can face harsh penalties, and where the failure is serious enough a manager may be given a suspended sentence rather than a fine. Read in that light, a rule that looks petty starts to look expensive. Nobody wrote it in order to irritate the workforce; somebody wrote it with a lawyer in the room, and the lawyer must have been thinking about what a court would say afterwards.

4The Osaka rule resists the obvious explanation. It can’t have been about laziness, since the same staff regularly work late without being asked twice. It might have been about the telephones, which somebody has to answer at one o’clock, or it could have been a way of protecting the younger employees from being sent out on errands during the only hour that belongs to them. Both readings fit the evidence; neither can be confirmed, and the company has never justified the working practice in writing.

5The London rule is the easiest to reconstruct and the least flattering. Somebody must have complained about one particular colleague. The agency can’t have wanted to accuse that person openly, because a direct conversation would have identified the complainant as well. Writing a rule that applies to everybody was simpler than choosing to criticize one person for it, and it allowed the management to blame nobody in public while making the point in private. It may not have been fair, but it worked, and nobody in the office could have proved who it was aimed at.

6What all four have in common is that the rule is an answer to a question nobody wrote down. Regulations at work are the residue of incidents, and the incident is almost never recorded beside the regulation it produced. You can’t count on the reason surviving; you can only reconstruct it from the shape of what is left. And the reconstruction is worth doing, because the alternative — assuming that the rule must have been designed to annoy you — is usually wrong, and it is always the least interesting explanation available. Whoever wrote the rule could have added one sentence of explanation, and must have decided, for reasons of their own, not to.

5 · One solved example, step by step.
Worked example

The evidence. A notice appears on Monday: no drinks in the server room, and it applies to visitors and contractors as well.

Step 1 — what is certain? The rule is new, so something happened. Something must have happened last week.

Step 2 — what can be ruled out? Contractors are included, and contractors were not in the building last week. A contractor can’t have caused it.

Step 3 — what remains possible? Two readings survive the evidence, so neither gets must: Somebody may have spilt something, or the insurance might have been changed.

The rule behind it. Use must have only when the evidence leaves one answer. As soon as two answers survive, drop to may, might or could have.

1 · Read the explanation.
Guessing about the past

When you did not see something happen, English asks you to say how sure you are. The pattern is always the same: modal + have + past participle. The modal never changes; the certainty is carried entirely by which modal you choose.

Must have means the evidence leaves one explanation. Can’t have means the evidence rules an explanation out. May, might and could have mean the question is still open. There is no difference in meaning between those last three; might is slightly the most common in speech.

Three things that go wrong
  • No mustn’t have. The negative of must have is can’t have: They can’t have stopped the lunch break.
  • Must have is not had to. He must have left early is a guess. He had to leave early is a duty. Same word, opposite jobs.
  • Could have has two lives. She could have been asked can mean it was possible that she was asked, or that asking her was possible and nobody did it. Context decides, and the second reading usually carries criticism.

The exception worth learning

Needn’t have against didn’t need to. Both look like deduction and neither is. He needn’t have prosecuted means he did it and it was unnecessary. He didn’t need to prosecute usually means he did not do it, because there was no need. The first carries criticism; the second simply reports.

12 · Read this before the extra practice.
Deduction is not obligation

Must have, can’t have, might have say nothing about rules. They report how sure you are about something you did not see, on the strength of evidence you did see. Somebody must have spilt a drink on it means the stain leaves no other explanation. They can’t have stopped the lunch break means the evidence rules it out. It might have been a safety issue leaves the question open.

The negative of must have is not mustn’t have — that form does not exist in this meaning. To say you are sure something did not happen, use can’t have or couldn’t have. Keep the scale in mind: must have (certain it did) → may / might / could have (possible) → might just have (possible but unlikely) → can’t / couldn’t have (certain it did not).

The forms behind the meaning

Every one of these is modal + have + past participle, and the modal never changes its shape: She must have known, not She must has known. In speech have reduces to ’ve and sounds like of, which is why must of known appears in writing; it is always an error.

Two extensions worth having at B2. The passive: The colleagues could have been asked — modal + have been + past participle, when who did it is unknown or irrelevant. The continuous: She must have been working late — modal + have been + -ing, when your deduction is about an activity that was in progress rather than a completed act. Compare He must have written it (the text exists) with He must have been writing it (that is what he was doing at the time).

Do not confuse deduction with regret. You should have told me criticises a past action; You must have told me deduces that you did. Same shape, different job.

Errors to watch: He mustn’t have seen it → He can’t have seen it · She must have went → must have gone · They might have to leave early yesterday → They might have left early.
